Title: US Airline Complaint Statistics: DOT Data for 2026

## How Many Air Travel Complaints Does DOT Receive Each Year?
Three counting eras. Up to May 2023, DOT published complaints broken down by category. From June 2023 to July 2025, it published "submissions" (complaints, inquiries and opinions) without a category breakdown. Since DOT launched its Aviation Complaint, Enforcement, and Reporting System (ACERS) on 1 August 2025, it reports complaint cases separately from compliments and comments, and from the January 2026 data it breaks them into 12 categories that passengers pick themselves instead of DOT analysts. DOT notes that filing a complaint does not mean the airline broke the law.

## Monthly Complaint Cases Since DOT's New System Launched
ACERS gives the first like-for-like monthly series in more than two years. Monthly volumes swung from about 4,500 to more than 8,500 cases.
</> Embed
_**Source:** DOT, August to December 2025 submission data (April 2026); DOT ATCR editions covering January to July 2026 data (published March to September 2026). DOT revises some monthly counts, so the seven monthly figures add up to slightly more than its January to June total (43,184) plus July._
The quietest month was October 2025 with **4,513** cases, and the busiest was March 2026 with **8,571**, just ahead of July 2026 at **8,544**. Complaint cases averaged 5,816 a month from August to December 2025 and 7,390 a month from January to July 2026. Twelve months of data is not yet enough to separate seasonal peaks from a lasting rise.

## What Passengers Complain About Most in 2026
Across US airlines, foreign airlines and travel agents, refunds led with **12,557 cases** from January to June 2026. Flight schedule problems came second with **9,477**, and baggage third with **6,459**.
</> Embed
_**Source:** DOT, Air Travel Consumer Report, August 2026 (Table 2, January to June 2026). Categories are selected by the consumer._
Inside the flight schedule category, cancellations drew 3,744 cases, delays 2,991, missed connections 991 and tarmac delays 462. Baggage cases, at 15.0% of the total, sit alongside the airline-reported mishandling rates in our baggage mishandling statistics, and the cancellation cases mirror the patterns in our global flight cancellation data. For US airlines alone the order flips: flight problems lead with 7,505 cases (25.9%), just ahead of refunds with 7,308 (25.2%). Refunds top the overall table because 3,935 of the 12,042 cases about foreign airlines (32.7%) concern refunds.
Complaining to DOT is one route. If your flight departed the EU or UK, or landed there on an EU or UK airline, EU261 or UK261 may entitle you to up to 600 EUR (520 GBP) when the cause was within the airline's control.Check Your Flight

## How the Complaint Mix Has Shifted Since 2019
Before the pandemic, flight problems were the leading complaint and refunds a minor one. In 2020, refunds made up **87.3%** of everything DOT received.
</> Embed
_**Source:** DOT ATCR, February 2021 (2019) and February 2022 (2020, 2021); DOT press release, 12 April 2023 (2022); DOT ATCR, August 2026 (January to June 2026). 2022 flight problems include claims for costs linked to flight problems. DOT published no category data for June 2023 to July 2025. Categories up to 2022 were assigned by DOT analysts; 2026 categories are chosen by passengers._
Refunds fell back to 59.1% in 2021 and 25.7% in 2022, when flight problems returned to the top with 31.7%. In January to June 2026, refunds lead again with 29.1%, ahead of flight schedule problems at 21.9%. The OIG found that DOT received more than 139,000 refund complaints from 2020 to 2022. One caution: before the switch, DOT analysts coded complaints, while in ACERS passengers choose the category themselves, and DOT has told airlines that some passengers pick categories their written complaint does not support, one reason it redesigned the complaint form on 10 February 2026.

## Which US Airlines Get the Most Complaints?
DOT lists every US airline that drew at least five complaint cases. From January to June 2026, **American Airlines had 9,046**, followed by Delta Air Lines with 4,534 and United Airlines with 4,524.
</> Embed
_**Source:** DOT, Air Travel Consumer Report, August 2026 (Table 3, January to June 2026). Passengers usually file against the airline brand on their ticket, so counts can include flights run by regional partners; Hawaiian Airlines is included in Alaska Airlines._
Raw counts largely follow size. American was also the biggest of DOT's reporting carriers by passengers, with 101.3 million enplaned in the same period, and our largest North American airlines ranking shows how the carriers compare in size. Frontier Airlines (3,673) and Spirit Airlines (2,053) drew more complaint cases relative to their passenger numbers than the larger carriers, which AirAdvisor's per-passenger calculation in the next chart shows. Each figure is a count of complaints filed with DOT, which describes its complaint data as based on consumer perception.

## Complaints per 100,000 Passengers by US Airline
DOT's current tables give counts only, so AirAdvisor divided each reporting carrier's complaint cases by the passengers DOT reports it enplaned from January to June 2026. **Spirit Airlines (27.8)** and **Frontier Airlines (21.1)** had the highest rates; **Southwest Airlines (1.5)** had the lowest.
</> Embed
_**Source:** AirAdvisor calculation from DOT ATCR, August 2026: complaint cases (Table 3, January to June 2026) divided by enplaned passengers in the denied boarding table for reporting marketing carriers (January to June 2026), times 100,000. Covers all 9 carriers DOT reports as marketing carriers, including branded regional partners._
Across the 9 carriers combined, AirAdvisor's calculation gives **6.5** complaint cases per 100,000 passengers, so Southwest's rate was less than a quarter of it and Spirit's more than four times it. Spirit stopped flying on 2 May 2026, so its passenger count covers about four months while complaints kept arriving; 680 of its 2,053 cases were about refunds. JetBlue (9.9) and American (8.9) were the only other carriers above that combined rate. The passenger base excludes inbound international passengers, which raises the rate for airlines with large international networks.

## Outlook
Complaint cases are running at about **7,390 a month** in 2026, against 5,816 a month in late 2025, and DOT now publishes 2026 complaint cases in 12 categories for every listed airline, the more detailed data it promised when ACERS launched. On 24 April 2026, DOT issued a final rule requiring covered airlines to file a one-page summary of passenger rights on delays, cancellations, baggage and boarding and to post it on their websites. Its Aviation Consumer Protection Advisory Committee was scheduled to meet on 22 and 23 September 2026 to discuss that summary and the airline customer service dashboards required by the 2024 FAA Reauthorization Act. For the scale of the delays behind many of these complaints, see our flight delay passenger impact statistics.

## Methodology Note
All complaint figures come from DOT, which counts written complaints to its Office of Aviation Consumer Protection, not complaints made to airlines. Yearly totals use the newest DOT figure for each year: 15,342 for 2019 (ATCR, February 2021), 102,560, 49,991 and 77,656 for 2020 to 2022 (DOT, April 2023), 96,853 submissions for 2023 and 97,906 for 2024. Earlier editions show slightly different values (102,550 for 2020 and 49,958 for 2021), and the OIG cites 15,332 for 2019; category shares for 2021 use the 49,958 base published with that year's categories. DOT also reports 86,240 submissions for 2022, a wider measure than the 77,656 complaints. The 2025 figure combines 49,502 legacy submissions (January to July, summed from seven monthly files) with 29,080 ACERS complaint cases (August to December), and the January to July 2026 total adds the published January to June figure (43,184) to July (8,544). April 2026 (7,278) comes from the June 2026 ATCR. Because DOT revises some monthly counts, the seven monthly figures sum to 51,739, slightly above the 51,728 year-to-date total used in the text. Complaints per 100,000 passengers are AirAdvisor calculations: January to June 2026 complaint cases for each of the 9 reporting marketing carriers divided by the enplaned passengers DOT reports for them in the same edition's denied boarding table, which counts domestic and outbound international passengers but not inbound international ones; DOT's own pre-2023 rankings used a different base, so the rates are not comparable with them. Rankings refer only to the dataset, period and metric named.

## Methodology Note
Complaints reflect passengers' perceptions, are attributed to the airline brand on the ticket, and in ACERS are categorised by the passengers themselves.

## Air Travel Consumer Report: June-December 2023, Full Year 2023 Airline Consumer Submissions Data
WASHINGTON – The U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT) today released data on the submissions (complaints, inquiries, and opinions) it has received from consumers about air travel for June-December 2023 and the full calendar year 2023. The submissions about air travel in calendar year 2023 are the highest number on record except for calendar year 2020.
The release of the submissions data in the Air Travel Consumer Report (ATCR) was delayed primarily because of the high volume of complaints against airlines and ticket agents received by the Office of Aviation Consumer Protection (OACP) and the time needed to review and process these consumer complaints using the Department’s outdated legacy consumer complaint application system. Over the past three years, complaints made up an average of 91% of consumer submissions.
The Department has been actively working on modernizing its system for handling consumer complaints with the support of a Technology Modernization Fund (TMF) investment to improve the customer experience for the tens of thousands of consumers who use the system each year. The modernization of the system will also enable OACP to engage in oversight of the airline industry more effectively.
As DOT modernizes its system, given the continued high volume of air travel service complaints concerning airlines and ticket agents, DOT has revised how it processes consumer complaints for efficiency which has resulted in less granular data being available in the ATCR. Except for displaying civil rights complaints in a similar manner as before, the ATCR displays consumer submissions (complaints, inquiries, and opinions) as opposed to complaints for June-December 2023 and compares submissions received in 2023 to the total submissions received for the same period in 2022. The Department will revert to displaying detailed complaint data in the ATCR in a similar manner as before once its new modernized system is operational.
**Calendar Year 2023**
In calendar year 2023, DOT received 96,853 submissions, compared to 86,240 in calendar year 2022.

## Air Travel Consumer Report: June-December 2023, Full Year 2023 Airline Consumer Submissions Data
Of the 96,853 submissions received in 2023, 67,661 concerned U.S. carriers, 24,991 concerned foreign air carriers, and 3,162 concerned travel companies.
In calendar year 2023, the Department received a total of 2,685 disability-related complaints, up from the total of 2,098 complaints received in calendar year 2022.
In calendar year 2023, the Department received a total of 223 discrimination-related complaints, up from the total of 176 complaints received in calendar year 2022.
**June 2023**
In June 2023, DOT received 9,204 airline service submissions, compared to 6,552 submissions in June 2022.
Of the 9,204 submissions received in June 2023, 6,847 concerned U.S. carriers, 2,059 concerned foreign air carriers, and 242 concerned travel companies.
In June 2023, the Department received a total of 278 disability-related complaints, up from the total of 175 complaints received in June 2022.
In June 2023, the Department received a total of 33 discrimination-related complaints, up from the total of 15 complaints received in June 2022.
**July 2023**
In July 2023, DOT received 12,590 airline service submissions, compared to 7,607 submissions in July 2022.
Of the 12,590 submissions received in July 2023, 9,714 concerned U.S. carriers, 2,569 concerned foreign air carriers, and 217 concerned travel companies.
In July 2023, the Department received a total of 300 disability-related complaints, up from the total of 248 complaints received in July 2022.

## Air Travel Consumer Report: June-December 2023, Full Year 2023 Airline Consumer Submissions Data
In July 2023, the Department received a total of four discrimination-related complaints, down from the total of 13 complaints received in July 2022.
**August 2023**
In August 2023, DOT received 10,132 airline service submissions, compared to 8,076 submissions in August 2022.
Of the 10,132 submissions received in August 2023, 7,348 concerned U.S. carriers, 2,472 concerned foreign air carriers, and 203 concerned travel companies.
In August 2023, the Department received a total of 287 disability-related complaints, up from the total of 196 complaints received in August 2022.
In August 2023, the Department received a total of 18 discrimination-related complaints, up from the total of 14 complaints received in August 2022.
**September 2023**
In September 2023, DOT received 7,510 airline service submissions, compared to 6,933 submissions in September 2022.
Of the 7,510 submissions received in September 2023, 5,125 concerned U.S. carriers, 2,128 concerned foreign air carriers, and 169 concerned travel companies.
In September 2023, the Department received a total of 158 disability-related complaints, down from the total of 187 complaints received in September 2022.
In September 2023, the Department received a total of 13 discrimination-related complaints, up from the total of 12 complaints received in September 2022.
**October 2023**
In October 2023, DOT received 5,783 airline service submissions, compared to 6,239 submissions in October 2022.

## Air Travel Consumer Report: June-December 2023, Full Year 2023 Airline Consumer Submissions Data
Of the 5,783 submissions received in October 2023, 3,719 concerned U.S. carriers, 1,806 concerned foreign air carriers, and 165 concerned travel companies.
In October 2023, the Department received a total of 202 disability-related complaints, down from the total of 206 complaints received in October 2022.
In October 2023, the Department received a total of 17 discrimination-related complaints, up from the total of 16 complaints received in October 2022.
**November 2023**
In November 2023, DOT received 4,783 airline service submissions, compared to 7,392 submissions in November 2022.
Of the 4,783 submissions received in November 2023, 3,052 concerned U.S. carriers, 1,514 concerned foreign air carriers, and 142 concerned travel companies.
In November 2023, the Department received a total of 185 disability-related complaints, up from the total of 164 complaints received in November 2022.
In November 2023, the Department received a total of 35 discrimination-related complaints, up from the total of 11 complaints received in November 2022.
**December 2023**
In December 2023, DOT received 5,442 airline service submissions, compared to 17,832 submissions in December 2022.
Of the 5,442 submissions received in December 2023, 3,368 concerned U.S. carriers, 1,855 concerned foreign air carriers, and 136 concerned travel companies.
In December 2023, the Department received a total of 202 disability-related complaints, down from the total of 218 complaints received in December 2022.

## Air Travel Consumer Report: June-December 2023, Full Year 2023 Airline Consumer Submissions Data
In December 2023, the Department received a total of 12 discrimination-related complaints, up from the total of nine complaints received in December 2022.
**DOT’s Historic Record of Consumer Protection Under the Biden-Harris Administration**
Under the Biden-Harris Administration, DOT has advanced the largest expansion of airline passenger rights, issued the biggest fines against airlines for failing consumers, and secured returns of more money to passengers in refunds and reimbursements than ever before in the Department’s history.

## Air Travel Consumer Report: June-December 2023, Full Year 2023 Airline Consumer Submissions Data
*   DOT announced a final rule that requires airlines to provide automatic cash refunds to passengers when owed and another final rule to protect consumers from costly surprise airline fees. These rules significantly expand consumer protections in air travel, provide passengers an easier pathway to refunds when owed, and save consumers more than half a billion dollars every year in hidden and surprise junk fees. Provisions of the final rule on airline refunds were fortified through the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 (Public Law 118-63) that President Biden signed into law on May 16, 2024.

*   In 2022, under Secretary Buttigieg’s guidance, DOT created an Airline Customer Service Dashboard known as FlightRights.gov to help airline passengers understand what they are entitled to receive when a delay or cancellation was within the airlines’ control and create standards that the Department can enforce. Now all 10 major U.S. airlines guarantee free rebooking and meals, and nine guarantee hotel accommodations when an airline issue causes a significant delay or cancellation. These are new commitments the airlines added to their customer service plans that DOT can legally ensure they adhere to and are displayed on flightrights.gov.

*   Since President Biden took office, DOT has helped oversee the return of almost $4 billion in refunds and reimbursements owed to airline passengers – including more than $600 million to passengers affected by the Southwest Airlines holiday meltdown in 2022.  
*   Under Secretary Buttigieg, DOT has issued more than $166 million in penalties against airlines for consumer protection violations. Between 1996 and 2020, DOT collectively issued less than $71 million in penalties against airlines for consumer protection violations.

*   DOT launched a new partnership with a bipartisan group of state attorneys general to fast-track the review of consumer complaints, hold airlines accountable, and protect the rights of the traveling public.
​​​​​​​
*   In 2023, the flight cancellation rate in the U.S. was a record low at under 1.2% – the lowest rate of flight cancellations in over 10 years despite a record amount of air travel.

*   DOT is undertaking its first ever industry-wide review of airline privacy practices and its first review of airline loyalty programs.

## Air Travel Consumer Report: June-December 2023, Full Year 2023 Airline Consumer Submissions Data
In addition to finalizing the rules to require automatic refunds and protect consumers from surprise fees, DOT is also pursuing rulemakings that would:
*   Propose to ban family seating junk fees and guarantee that parents can sit with their children for no extra charge when they fly. Before President Biden and Secretary Buttigieg pressed airlines last year, no airline committed to guaranteeing fee-free family seating. Now, four airlines guarantee fee-free family seating, as the Department is working on its family seating junk fee ban proposal.

*   Propose to make passenger compensation and amenities mandatory so that travelers are taken care of when airlines cause flight delays or cancellations.

*   Expand the rights for passengers who use wheelchairs and ensure that they can travel safely and with dignity.
Consumers may file air travel consumer or civil rights complaints online at https://secure.dot.gov/air-travel-complaint, or they may mail a complaint to the Office of Aviation Consumer Protection, U.S. Department of Transportation, C-70, W96-432, 1200 New Jersey Avenue, SE, Washington, DC 20590.
The ATCR and other aviation consumer matters of interest to the public can be found at https://www.transportation.gov/airconsumer.

## Air Travel Consumer Report: June-December 2023, Full Year 2023 Airline Consumer Submissions Data
*   DOT announced a final rule that requires airlines to provide automatic cash refunds to passengers when owed and another final rule to protect consumers from costly surprise airline fees. These rules significantly expand consumer protections in air travel, provide passengers an easier pathway to refunds when owed, and save consumers more than half a billion dollars every year in hidden and surprise junk fees. Provisions of the final rule on airline refunds were fortified through the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 (Public Law 118-63) that President Biden signed into law on May 16, 2024.

*   In 2022, under Secretary Buttigieg’s guidance, DOT created an Airline Customer Service Dashboard known as FlightRights.gov to help airline passengers understand what they are entitled to receive when a delay or cancellation was within the airlines’ control and create standards that the Department can enforce. Now all 10 major U.S. airlines guarantee free rebooking and meals, and nine guarantee hotel accommodations when an airline issue causes a significant delay or cancellation. These are new commitments the airlines added to their customer service plans that DOT can legally ensure they adhere to and are displayed on flightrights.gov.

*   Since President Biden took office, DOT has helped oversee the return of almost $4 billion in refunds and reimbursements owed to airline passengers – including more than $600 million to passengers affected by the Southwest Airlines holiday meltdown in 2022.  
*   Under Secretary Buttigieg, DOT has issued more than $166 million in penalties against airlines for consumer protection violations. Between 1996 and 2020, DOT collectively issued less than $71 million in penalties against airlines for consumer protection violations.

*   DOT launched a new partnership with a bipartisan group of state attorneys general to fast-track the review of consumer complaints, hold airlines accountable, and protect the rights of the traveling public.
​​​​​​​
*   In 2023, the flight cancellation rate in the U.S. was a record low at under 1.2% – the lowest rate of flight cancellations in over 10 years despite a record amount of air travel.

*   DOT is undertaking its first ever industry-wide review of airline privacy practices and its first review of airline loyalty programs.

## How Many Air Travel Complaints Does DOT Receive Each Year?
Three counting eras. Up to May 2023, DOT published complaints broken down by category. From June 2023 to July 2025, it published "submissions" (complaints, inquiries and opinions) without a category breakdown. Since DOT launched its Aviation Complaint, Enforcement, and Reporting System (ACERS) on 1 August 2025, it reports complaint cases separately from compliments and comments, and from the January 2026 data it breaks them into 12 categories that passengers pick themselves instead of DOT analysts. DOT notes that filing a complaint does not mean the airline broke the law.
texts.6:
## Monthly Complaint Cases Since DOT's New System Launched
ACERS gives the first like-for-like monthly series in more than two years. Monthly volumes swung from about 4,500 to more than 8,500 cases.
</> Embed
_**Source:** DOT, August to December 2025 submission data (April 2026); DOT ATCR editions covering January to July 2026 data (published March to September 2026). DOT revises some monthly counts, so the seven monthly figures add up to slightly more than its January to June total (43,184) plus July._
The quietest month was October 2025 with **4,513** cases, and the busiest was March 2026 with **8,571**, just ahead of July 2026 at **8,544**. Complaint cases averaged 5,816 a month from August to December 2025 and 7,390 a month from January to July 2026. Twelve months of data is not yet enough to separate seasonal peaks from a lasting rise.
texts.7:
## What Passengers Complain About Most in 2026
Across US airlines, foreign airlines and travel agents, refunds led with **12,557 cases** from January to June 2026. Flight schedule problems came second with **9,477**, and baggage third with **6,459**.
</> Embed
_**Source:** DOT, Air Travel Consumer Report, August 2026 (Table 2, January to June 2026). Categories are selected by the consumer._
Inside the flight schedule category, cancellations drew 3,744 cases, delays 2,991, missed connections 991 and tarmac delays 462. Baggage cases, at 15.0% of the total, sit alongside the airline-reported mishandling rates in our baggage mishandling statistics, and the cancellation cases mirror the patterns in our global flight cancellation data. For US airlines alone the order flips: flight problems lead with 7,505 cases (25.9%), just ahead of refunds with 7,308 (25.2%). Refunds top the overall table because 3,935 of the 12,042 cases about foreign airlines (32.7%) concern refunds.
Complaining to DOT is one route. If your flight departed the EU or UK, or landed there on an EU or UK airline, EU261 or UK261 may entitle you to up to 600 EUR (520 GBP) when the cause was within the airline's control.Check Your Flight
texts.8:
## How the Complaint Mix Has Shifted Since 2019
Before the pandemic, flight problems were the leading complaint and refunds a minor one. In 2020, refunds made up **87.3%** of everything DOT received.
</> Embed
_**Source:** DOT ATCR, February 2021 (2019) and February 2022 (2020, 2021); DOT press release, 12 April 2023 (2022); DOT ATCR, August 2026 (January to June 2026). 2022 flight problems include claims for costs linked to flight problems. DOT published no category data for June 2023 to July 2025. Categories up to 2022 were assigned by DOT analysts; 2026 categories are chosen by passengers._
Refunds fell back to 59.1% in 2021 and 25.7% in 2022, when flight problems returned to the top with 31.7%. In January to June 2026, refunds lead again with 29.1%, ahead of flight schedule problems at 21.9%. The OIG found that DOT received more than 139,000 refund complaints from 2020 to 2022. One caution: before the switch, DOT analysts coded complaints, while in ACERS passengers choose the category themselves, and DOT has told airlines that some passengers pick categories their written complaint does not support, one reason it redesigned the complaint form on 10 February 2026.
texts.9:
## Which US Airlines Get the Most Complaints?
DOT lists every US airline that drew at least five complaint cases. From January to June 2026, **American Airlines had 9,046**, followed by Delta Air Lines with 4,534 and United Airlines with 4,524.
</> Embed
_**Source:** DOT, Air Travel Consumer Report, August 2026 (Table 3, January to June 2026). Passengers usually file against the airline brand on their ticket, so counts can include flights run by regional partners; Hawaiian Airlines is included in Alaska Airlines._
Raw counts largely follow size. American was also the biggest of DOT's reporting carriers by passengers, with 101.3 million enplaned in the same period, and our largest North American airlines ranking shows how the carriers compare in size. Frontier Airlines (3,673) and Spirit Airlines (2,053) drew more complaint cases relative to their passenger numbers than the larger carriers, which AirAdvisor's per-passenger calculation in the next chart shows. Each figure is a count of complaints filed with DOT, which describes its complaint data as based on consumer perception.
texts.10:
## Complaints per 100,000 Passengers by US Airline
DOT's current tables give counts only, so AirAdvisor divided each reporting carrier's complaint cases by the passengers DOT reports it enplaned from January to June 2026. **Spirit Airlines (27.8)** and **Frontier Airlines (21.1)** had the highest rates; **Southwest Airlines (1.5)** had the lowest.
</> Embed
_**Source:** AirAdvisor calculation from DOT ATCR, August 2026: complaint cases (Table 3, January to June 2026) divided by enplaned passengers in the denied boarding table for reporting marketing carriers (January to June 2026), times 100,000. Covers all 9 carriers DOT reports as marketing carriers, including branded regional partners._
Across the 9 carriers combined, AirAdvisor's calculation gives **6.5** complaint cases per 100,000 passengers, so Southwest's rate was less than a quarter of it and Spirit's more than four times it. Spirit stopped flying on 2 May 2026, so its passenger count covers about four months while complaints kept arriving; 680 of its 2,053 cases were about refunds. JetBlue (9.9) and American (8.9) were the only other carriers above that combined rate. The passenger base excludes inbound international passengers, which raises the rate for airlines with large international networks.
texts.15:
## Outlook
Complaint cases are running at about **7,390 a month** in 2026, against 5,816 a month in late 2025, and DOT now publishes 2026 complaint cases in 12 categories for every listed airline, the more detailed data it promised when ACERS launched. On 24 April 2026, DOT issued a final rule requiring covered airlines to file a one-page summary of passenger rights on delays, cancellations, baggage and boarding and to post it on their websites. Its Aviation Consumer Protection Advisory Committee was scheduled to meet on 22 and 23 September 2026 to discuss that summary and the airline customer service dashboards required by the 2024 FAA Reauthorization Act. For the scale of the delays behind many of these complaints, see our flight delay passenger impact statistics.

## Methodology Note
All complaint figures come from DOT, which counts written complaints to its Office of Aviation Consumer Protection, not complaints made to airlines. Yearly totals use the newest DOT figure for each year: 15,342 for 2019 (ATCR, February 2021), 102,560, 49,991 and 77,656 for 2020 to 2022 (DOT, April 2023), 96,853 submissions for 2023 and 97,906 for 2024. Earlier editions show slightly different values (102,550 for 2020 and 49,958 for 2021), and the OIG cites 15,332 for 2019; category shares for 2021 use the 49,958 base published with that year's categories. DOT also reports 86,240 submissions for 2022, a wider measure than the 77,656 complaints. The 2025 figure combines 49,502 legacy submissions (January to July, summed from seven monthly files) with 29,080 ACERS complaint cases (August to December), and the January to July 2026 total adds the published January to June figure (43,184) to July (8,544). April 2026 (7,278) comes from the June 2026 ATCR. Because DOT revises some monthly counts, the seven monthly figures sum to 51,739, slightly above the 51,728 year-to-date total used in the text. Complaints per 100,000 passengers are AirAdvisor calculations: January to June 2026 complaint cases for each of the 9 reporting marketing carriers divided by the enplaned passengers DOT reports for them in the same edition's denied boarding table, which counts domestic and outbound international passengers but not inbound international ones; DOT's own pre-2023 rankings used a different base, so the rates are not comparable with them. Rankings refer only to the dataset, period and metric named.

Three counting eras. Up to May 2023, DOT published complaints broken down by category. Since DOT launched its Aviation Complaint, Enforcement, and Reporting System (ACERS) on 1 August 2025, it reports complaint cases separately from compliments and comments, and from the January 2026 data it breaks them into 12 categories that passengers pick themselves instead of DOT analysts. DOT notes that filing a complaint does not mean the airline broke the law.

## Monthly Complaint Cases Since DOT's New System Launched
ACERS gives the first like-for-like monthly series in more than two years. Monthly volumes swung from about 4,500 to more than 8,500 cases.
</> Embed
_**Source:** DOT, August to December 2025 submission data (April 2026); DOT ATCR editions covering January to July 2026 data (published March to September 2026). DOT revises some monthly counts, so the seven monthly figures add up to slightly more than its January to June total (43,184) plus July._
The quietest month was October 2025 with **4,513** cases, and the busiest was March 2026 with **8,571**, just ahead of July 2026 at **8,544**. Complaint cases averaged 5,816 a month from August to December 2025 and 7,390 a month from January to July 2026. Twelve months of data is not yet enough to separate seasonal peaks from a lasting rise.

## What Passengers Complain About Most in 2026
Across US airlines, foreign airlines and travel agents, refunds led with **12,557 cases** from January to June 2026. Flight schedule problems came second with **9,477**, and baggage third with **6,459**.
</> Embed
_**Source:** DOT, Air Travel Consumer Report, August 2026 (Table 2, January to June 2026). Categories are selected by the consumer._
Inside the flight schedule category, cancellations drew 3,744 cases, delays 2,991, missed connections 991 and tarmac delays 462. Baggage cases, at 15.0% of the total, sit alongside the airline-reported mishandling rates in our baggage mishandling statistics, and the cancellation cases mirror the patterns in our global flight cancellation data. For US airlines alone the order flips: flight problems lead with 7,505 cases (25.9%), just ahead of refunds with 7,308 (25.2%). Refunds top the overall table because 3,935 of the 12,042 cases about foreign airlines (32.7%) concern refunds.
Complaining to DOT is one route. If your flight departed the EU or UK, or landed there on an EU or UK airline, EU261 or UK261 may entitle you to up to 600 EUR (520 GBP) when the cause was within the airline's control.Check Your Flight

## How the Complaint Mix Has Shifted Since 2019
Before the pandemic, flight problems were the leading complaint and refunds a minor one. In 2020, refunds made up **87.3%** of everything DOT received.
</> Embed
_**Source:** DOT ATCR, February 2021 (2019) and February 2022 (2020, 2021); DOT press release, 12 April 2023 (2022); DOT ATCR, August 2026 (January to June 2026). 2022 flight problems include claims for costs linked to flight problems. DOT published no category data for June 2023 to July 2025. Categories up to 2022 were assigned by DOT analysts; 2026 categories are chosen by passengers._
Refunds fell back to 59.1% in 2021 and 25.7% in 2022, when flight problems returned to the top with 31.7%. In January to June 2026, refunds lead again with 29.1%, ahead of flight schedule problems at 21.9%. The OIG found that DOT received more than 139,000 refund complaints from 2020 to 2022. One caution: before the switch, DOT analysts coded complaints, while in ACERS passengers choose the category themselves, and DOT has told airlines that some passengers pick categories their written complaint does not support, one reason it redesigned the complaint form on 10 February 2026.

## Which US Airlines Get the Most Complaints?
DOT lists every US airline that drew at least five complaint cases. From January to June 2026, **American Airlines had 9,046**, followed by Delta Air Lines with 4,534 and United Airlines with 4,524.
</> Embed
_**Source:** DOT, Air Travel Consumer Report, August 2026 (Table 3, January to June 2026). Passengers usually file against the airline brand on their ticket, so counts can include flights run by regional partners; Hawaiian Airlines is included in Alaska Airlines._
Raw counts largely follow size. American was also the biggest of DOT's reporting carriers by passengers, with 101.3 million enplaned in the same period, and our largest North American airlines ranking shows how the carriers compare in size. Frontier Airlines (3,673) and Spirit Airlines (2,053) drew more complaint cases relative to their passenger numbers than the larger carriers, which AirAdvisor's per-passenger calculation in the next chart shows. Each figure is a count of complaints filed with DOT, which describes its complaint data as based on consumer perception.

## Complaints per 100,000 Passengers by US Airline
DOT's current tables give counts only, so AirAdvisor divided each reporting carrier's complaint cases by the passengers DOT reports it enplaned from January to June 2026. **Spirit Airlines (27.8)** and **Frontier Airlines (21.1)** had the highest rates; **Southwest Airlines (1.5)** had the lowest.
</> Embed
_**Source:** AirAdvisor calculation from DOT ATCR, August 2026: complaint cases (Table 3, January to June 2026) divided by enplaned passengers in the denied boarding table for reporting marketing carriers (January to June 2026), times 100,000. Covers all 9 carriers DOT reports as marketing carriers, including branded regional partners._
Across the 9 carriers combined, AirAdvisor's calculation gives **6.5** complaint cases per 100,000 passengers, so Southwest's rate was less than a quarter of it and Spirit's more than four times it. Spirit stopped flying on 2 May 2026, so its passenger count covers about four months while complaints kept arriving; 680 of its 2,053 cases were about refunds. JetBlue (9.9) and American (8.9) were the only other carriers above that combined rate. The passenger base excludes inbound international passengers, which raises the rate for airlines with large international networks.

## Outlook
Complaint cases are running at about **7,390 a month** in 2026, against 5,816 a month in late 2025, and DOT now publishes 2026 complaint cases in 12 categories for every listed airline, the more detailed data it promised when ACERS launched. On 24 April 2026, DOT issued a final rule requiring covered airlines to file a one-page summary of passenger rights on delays, cancellations, baggage and boarding and to post it on their websites. Its Aviation Consumer Protection Advisory Committee was scheduled to meet on 22 and 23 September 2026 to discuss that summary and the airline customer service dashboards required by the 2024 FAA Reauthorization Act. For the scale of the delays behind many of these complaints, see our flight delay passenger impact statistics.

## Methodology Note
All complaint figures come from DOT, which counts written complaints to its Office of Aviation Consumer Protection, not complaints made to airlines. Yearly totals use the newest DOT figure for each year: 15,342 for 2019 (ATCR, February 2021), 102,560, 49,991 and 77,656 for 2020 to 2022 (DOT, April 2023), 96,853 submissions for 2023 and 97,906 for 2024. Earlier editions show slightly different values (102,550 for 2020 and 49,958 for 2021), and the OIG cites 15,332 for 2019; category shares for 2021 use the 49,958 base published with that year's categories. DOT also reports 86,240 submissions for 2022, a wider measure than the 77,656 complaints. The 2025 figure combines 49,502 legacy submissions (January to July, summed from seven monthly files) with 29,080 ACERS complaint cases (August to December), and the January to July 2026 total adds the published January to June figure (43,184) to July (8,544). April 2026 (7,278) comes from the June 2026 ATCR. Because DOT revises some monthly counts, the seven monthly figures sum to 51,739, slightly above the 51,728 year-to-date total used in the text. Complaints per 100,000 passengers are AirAdvisor calculations: January to June 2026 complaint cases for each of the 9 reporting marketing carriers divided by the enplaned passengers DOT reports for them in the same edition's denied boarding table, which counts domestic and outbound international passengers but not inbound international ones; DOT's own pre-2023 rankings used a different base, so the rates are not comparable with them. Rankings refer only to the dataset, period and metric named.

## Methodology Note
Complaints reflect passengers' perceptions, are attributed to the airline brand on the ticket, and in ACERS are categorised by the passengers themselves.

**Air Travel Consumer Report: June 2023 and 2nd Quarter 2023 Numbers**
WASHINGTON – The U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT) today released its Air Travel Consumer Report (ATCR) on airline operational data compiled for the month of June 2023 and the first six months of 2023 for on-time performance, mishandled baggage, mishandled wheelchairs and scooters, and second quarter oversales.
The ATCR is designed to assist consumers with information on the quality of services provided by airlines. DOT remains committed to ensuring airline passengers are treated fairly and flights operate as scheduled.**For the first six months of 2023, 1.6% of flights have been canceled, far below the 3.2% cancellation rate for the first six months of last year and the 2.4% cancellation rate for first six months of pre-pandemic 2019.**
DOT uses the data from the ATCR, consumer complaints, and other information it secures from the airlines to inform its enforcement activities and the adequacy of existing rules.
This year, DOT has already issued the largest fines in the history of the consumer protection office primarily based on complaints received. Since the pandemic began, the Department has helped return more than $2.5 billion in refunds to travelers.
The Department is also enhancing consumer protections through rulemakings and other activities. After a two-year DOT push to improve the passenger experience, the 10 largest airlines now guarantee meals and free rebooking on the same airline and nine guarantee hotel accommodations as part of the Department’s Airline Customer Service Dashboard. DOT expanded the user-friendly dashboard at FlightRights.Gov to highlight which airlines, if any, offer cash compensation, provide travel credits or vouchers, or award frequent flyer miles when they cause flight delays or cancellations. In May, DOT announced plans to launch a new rulemaking that would propose to make passenger compensation and amenities mandatory so that travelers are taken care of when airlines cause flight delays or cancellations, such as staffing issues or mechanical problems.

Further, earlier this year, President Biden and Secretary Buttigieg pressed airlines to commit to fee-free family seating. Before their urging, no airline committed to guaranteeing fee-free family seating. Now three airlines have committed to guaranteeing fee-free family seating, and DOT is pursuing a rulemaking that would require all airlines to do so. Secretary Buttigieg also submitted to Congress a legislative proposal to require that airlines provide fee-free family seating.
To further assist consumers in assessing airline family seating commitments, in March 2023, DOT rolled out a new family seating dashboard that highlights the airlines that guarantee fee-free family seating, and those that do not, making it easier for parents to avoid paying junk fees to sit with their children when they fly.
**Flight Operations**
The 600,721 flights operated in June 2023 were 102.94% of the 583,584 flights operated in June 2022. Operated flights in June 2023 were up 2.94% year-over-year from the 583,584 flights operated in June 2022 and down 1.97% month-over-month from 612,797 flights operated in May 2023.
In June 2023, the 10 marketing network carriers reported 613,577 scheduled domestic flights, 12,856 (2.1%) of which were canceled. In May 2023, airlines scheduled 616,630 domestic flights, of which 3,833 (0.6%) were canceled. In June 2022, airlines scheduled 602,057 domestic flights, of which 18,473 (3.1%) were canceled.
**June 2023 On-Time Arrival**
In June 2023, reporting marketing carriers posted an on-time arrival rate of 71.3% down from both 81.2% in May 2023 and 73.5% in June 2022. The year-to-date on-time arrival rate for 2023 is 76.5%.
Highest Marketing Carrier On-Time Arrival Rates June 2023 (ATCR Table 1)

1.   Alaska Airlines Network – 79.4%   
2.   Delta Air Lines Network – 77.8%   
3.   Hawaiian Airlines – 77.4%
Lowest Marketing Carrier On-Time Arrival Rates June 2023 (ATCR Table 1)
1.   Frontier Airlines – 53.7%   
2.   Spirit Airlines – 58.8%   
3.   JetBlue Airways – 60.8%
For the first six months of 2023, the reporting marketing carriers posted an on-time arrival rate of 76.48%, up from 75.94% for the same period in 2022.
**June 2023 Flight Cancellations**
In June 2023, reporting marketing carriers canceled 2.1% of their scheduled domestic flights, higher than the rate 0.6% in May 2023 and lower than 3.1% in June 2022.
Lowest Marketing Carrier Rates of Canceled Flights June 2023 (ATCR Table 6)
1.   Alaska Airlines Network – 0.3%   
2.   Allegiant Air – 0.6%   
3.   Southwest Airlines – 0.6%
Highest Marketing Carrier Rates of Canceled Flights June 2023 (ATCR Table 6)
1.   United Airlines Network – 4.5%   
2.   Frontier Airlines – 3.9%   
3.   JetBlue Airways – 3.5%
For the first six months of 2023, the reporting marketing carriers posted a cancellation rate of 1.6%, down from 3.2% for the same period in 2022.
**Complaints About Airline Service**
The Department continues to receive a high volume of air travel service complaints against airlines and ticket agents and its Office of Aviation Consumer Protection is processing them. . The release of consumer complaint data in the ATCR has been delayed primarily because of the time needed to review and process these consumer complaints. The Department is examining how best to review and process the consumer complaints received to avoid reporting delays as it is increasingly clear that consumer complaints are not returning to pre-pandemic levels.
**Tarmac Delays**

In June 2023, airlines reported 74 tarmac delays of more than three hours on domestic flights, compared to three tarmac delays of more than three hours on domestic flights reported in May 2023. In June 2023, airlines reported 14 tarmac delays of more than four hours on international flights, compared to two tarmac delays reported in May 2023.
Airlines are required to have and adhere to assurances that they will not allow aircraft to remain on the tarmac for more than three hours for domestic flights and four hours for international flights without providing passengers the option to deplane, subject to exceptions related to safety, security, and Air Traffic Control related reasons. An exception also exists for departure delays if the airline begins to return the aircraft to a suitable disembarkation point to deplane passengers by those times.
The Department investigates extended tarmac delays.
**Mishandled Baggage**
In June 2023, reporting marketing carriers handled 43.4 million bags and posted a mishandled baggage rate of 0.70%, higher than the rate of 0.51% in May 2023 and lower than the rate of 0.71% in June 2022.
For the first half of 2023, the carriers posted a mishandled baggage rate of 0.61%, lower than the rate of 0.63% posted in the first half of 2022.
The Department began displaying the mishandled baggage data as a percentage (i.e., per 100 bags enplaned) in January 2022. This is consistent with the manner that the mishandled wheelchairs and scooters rate is calculated and displayed.
In the prior three calendar year reports (2019 to 2021), the Department calculated the mishandled baggage rate based on the number of mishandled bags per 1,000 checked bags.

## Air Travel Consumer Report: June-December 2023, Full Year 2023 Airline Consumer Submissions Data
WASHINGTON – The U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT) today released data on the submissions (complaints, inquiries, and opinions) it has received from consumers about air travel for June-December 2023 and the full calendar year 2023. The submissions about air travel in calendar year 2023 are the highest number on record except for calendar year 2020.
The release of the submissions data in the Air Travel Consumer Report (ATCR) was delayed primarily because of the high volume of complaints against airlines and ticket agents received by the Office of Aviation Consumer Protection (OACP) and the time needed to review and process these consumer complaints using the Department’s outdated legacy consumer complaint application system. Over the past three years, complaints made up an average of 91% of consumer submissions.
The Department has been actively working on modernizing its system for handling consumer complaints with the support of a Technology Modernization Fund (TMF) investment to improve the customer experience for the tens of thousands of consumers who use the system each year. The modernization of the system will also enable OACP to engage in oversight of the airline industry more effectively.
As DOT modernizes its system, given the continued high volume of air travel service complaints concerning airlines and ticket agents, DOT has revised how it processes consumer complaints for efficiency which has resulted in less granular data being available in the ATCR. Except for displaying civil rights complaints in a similar manner as before, the ATCR displays consumer submissions (complaints, inquiries, and opinions) as opposed to complaints for June-December 2023 and compares submissions received in 2023 to the total submissions received for the same period in 2022. The Department will revert to displaying detailed complaint data in the ATCR in a similar manner as before once its new modernized system is operational.
**Calendar Year 2023**
In calendar year 2023, DOT received 96,853 submissions, compared to 86,240 in calendar year 2022.

## Air Travel Consumer Report: June-December 2023, Full Year 2023 Airline Consumer Submissions Data
Of the 96,853 submissions received in 2023, 67,661 concerned U.S. carriers, 24,991 concerned foreign air carriers, and 3,162 concerned travel companies.
In calendar year 2023, the Department received a total of 2,685 disability-related complaints, up from the total of 2,098 complaints received in calendar year 2022.
In calendar year 2023, the Department received a total of 223 discrimination-related complaints, up from the total of 176 complaints received in calendar year 2022.
**June 2023**
In June 2023, DOT received 9,204 airline service submissions, compared to 6,552 submissions in June 2022.
Of the 9,204 submissions received in June 2023, 6,847 concerned U.S. carriers, 2,059 concerned foreign air carriers, and 242 concerned travel companies.
In June 2023, the Department received a total of 278 disability-related complaints, up from the total of 175 complaints received in June 2022.
In June 2023, the Department received a total of 33 discrimination-related complaints, up from the total of 15 complaints received in June 2022.
**July 2023**
In July 2023, DOT received 12,590 airline service submissions, compared to 7,607 submissions in July 2022.
Of the 12,590 submissions received in July 2023, 9,714 concerned U.S. carriers, 2,569 concerned foreign air carriers, and 217 concerned travel companies.
In July 2023, the Department received a total of 300 disability-related complaints, up from the total of 248 complaints received in July 2022.

## Air Travel Consumer Report: June-December 2023, Full Year 2023 Airline Consumer Submissions Data
In July 2023, the Department received a total of four discrimination-related complaints, down from the total of 13 complaints received in July 2022.
**August 2023**
In August 2023, DOT received 10,132 airline service submissions, compared to 8,076 submissions in August 2022.
Of the 10,132 submissions received in August 2023, 7,348 concerned U.S. carriers, 2,472 concerned foreign air carriers, and 203 concerned travel companies.
In August 2023, the Department received a total of 287 disability-related complaints, up from the total of 196 complaints received in August 2022.
In August 2023, the Department received a total of 18 discrimination-related complaints, up from the total of 14 complaints received in August 2022.
**September 2023**
In September 2023, DOT received 7,510 airline service submissions, compared to 6,933 submissions in September 2022.
Of the 7,510 submissions received in September 2023, 5,125 concerned U.S. carriers, 2,128 concerned foreign air carriers, and 169 concerned travel companies.
In September 2023, the Department received a total of 158 disability-related complaints, down from the total of 187 complaints received in September 2022.
In September 2023, the Department received a total of 13 discrimination-related complaints, up from the total of 12 complaints received in September 2022.
**October 2023**
In October 2023, DOT received 5,783 airline service submissions, compared to 6,239 submissions in October 2022.

## Air Travel Consumer Report: June-December 2023, Full Year 2023 Airline Consumer Submissions Data
Of the 5,783 submissions received in October 2023, 3,719 concerned U.S. carriers, 1,806 concerned foreign air carriers, and 165 concerned travel companies.
In October 2023, the Department received a total of 202 disability-related complaints, down from the total of 206 complaints received in October 2022.
In October 2023, the Department received a total of 17 discrimination-related complaints, up from the total of 16 complaints received in October 2022.
**November 2023**
In November 2023, DOT received 4,783 airline service submissions, compared to 7,392 submissions in November 2022.
Of the 4,783 submissions received in November 2023, 3,052 concerned U.S. carriers, 1,514 concerned foreign air carriers, and 142 concerned travel companies.
In November 2023, the Department received a total of 185 disability-related complaints, up from the total of 164 complaints received in November 2022.
In November 2023, the Department received a total of 35 discrimination-related complaints, up from the total of 11 complaints received in November 2022.
**December 2023**
In December 2023, DOT received 5,442 airline service submissions, compared to 17,832 submissions in December 2022.
Of the 5,442 submissions received in December 2023, 3,368 concerned U.S. carriers, 1,855 concerned foreign air carriers, and 136 concerned travel companies.
In December 2023, the Department received a total of 202 disability-related complaints, down from the total of 218 complaints received in December 2022.

The ATCR is designed to assist consumers with information on the quality of services provided by airlines.

## Air Travel Consumer Report: June-December 2023, Full Year 2023 Airline Consumer Submissions Data
WASHINGTON – The U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT) today released data on the submissions (complaints, inquiries, and opinions) it has received from consumers about air travel for June-December 2023 and the full calendar year 2023. The submissions about air travel in calendar year 2023 are the highest number on record except for calendar year 2020.
The release of the submissions data in the Air Travel Consumer Report (ATCR) was delayed primarily because of the high volume of complaints against airlines and ticket agents received by the Office of Aviation Consumer Protection (OACP) and the time needed to review and process these consumer complaints using the Department’s outdated legacy consumer complaint application system. Over the past three years, complaints made up an average of 91% of consumer submissions.
The Department has been actively working on modernizing its system for handling consumer complaints with the support of a Technology Modernization Fund (TMF) investment to improve the customer experience for the tens of thousands of consumers who use the system each year. The modernization of the system will also enable OACP to engage in oversight of the airline industry more effectively.
As DOT modernizes its system, given the continued high volume of air travel service complaints concerning airlines and ticket agents, DOT has revised how it processes consumer complaints for efficiency which has resulted in less granular data being available in the ATCR. Except for displaying civil rights complaints in a similar manner as before, the ATCR displays consumer submissions (complaints, inquiries, and opinions) as opposed to complaints for June-December 2023 and compares submissions received in 2023 to the total submissions received for the same period in 2022. The Department will revert to displaying detailed complaint data in the ATCR in a similar manner as before once its new modernized system is operational.

## How Many Air Travel Complaints Does DOT Receive Each Year?
Three counting eras. Up to May 2023, DOT published complaints broken down by category. From June 2023 to July 2025, it published "submissions" (complaints, inquiries and opinions) without a category breakdown. Since DOT launched its Aviation Complaint, Enforcement, and Reporting System (ACERS) on 1 August 2025, it reports complaint cases separately from compliments and comments, and from the January 2026 data it breaks them into 12 categories that passengers pick themselves instead of DOT analysts. DOT notes that filing a complaint does not mean the airline broke the law.

## Monthly Complaint Cases Since DOT's New System Launched
ACERS gives the first like-for-like monthly series in more than two years. Monthly volumes swung from about 4,500 to more than 8,500 cases.
</> Embed
_**Source:** DOT, August to December 2025 submission data (April 2026); DOT ATCR editions covering January to July 2026 data (published March to September 2026). DOT revises some monthly counts, so the seven monthly figures add up to slightly more than its January to June total (43,184) plus July._
The quietest month was October 2025 with **4,513** cases, and the busiest was March 2026 with **8,571**, just ahead of July 2026 at **8,544**. Complaint cases averaged 5,816 a month from August to December 2025 and 7,390 a month from January to July 2026. Twelve months of data is not yet enough to separate seasonal peaks from a lasting rise.

## What Passengers Complain About Most in 2026
Across US airlines, foreign airlines and travel agents, refunds led with **12,557 cases** from January to June 2026. Flight schedule problems came second with **9,477**, and baggage third with **6,459**.
</> Embed
_**Source:** DOT, Air Travel Consumer Report, August 2026 (Table 2, January to June 2026). Categories are selected by the consumer._
Inside the flight schedule category, cancellations drew 3,744 cases, delays 2,991, missed connections 991 and tarmac delays 462. Baggage cases, at 15.0% of the total, sit alongside the airline-reported mishandling rates in our baggage mishandling statistics, and the cancellation cases mirror the patterns in our global flight cancellation data. For US airlines alone the order flips: flight problems lead with 7,505 cases (25.9%), just ahead of refunds with 7,308 (25.2%). Refunds top the overall table because 3,935 of the 12,042 cases about foreign airlines (32.7%) concern refunds.
Complaining to DOT is one route. If your flight departed the EU or UK, or landed there on an EU or UK airline, EU261 or UK261 may entitle you to up to 600 EUR (520 GBP) when the cause was within the airline's control.Check Your Flight

## How the Complaint Mix Has Shifted Since 2019
Before the pandemic, flight problems were the leading complaint and refunds a minor one. In 2020, refunds made up **87.3%** of everything DOT received.
</> Embed
_**Source:** DOT ATCR, February 2021 (2019) and February 2022 (2020, 2021); DOT press release, 12 April 2023 (2022); DOT ATCR, August 2026 (January to June 2026). 2022 flight problems include claims for costs linked to flight problems. DOT published no category data for June 2023 to July 2025. Categories up to 2022 were assigned by DOT analysts; 2026 categories are chosen by passengers._
Refunds fell back to 59.1% in 2021 and 25.7% in 2022, when flight problems returned to the top with 31.7%. In January to June 2026, refunds lead again with 29.1%, ahead of flight schedule problems at 21.9%. The OIG found that DOT received more than 139,000 refund complaints from 2020 to 2022. One caution: before the switch, DOT analysts coded complaints, while in ACERS passengers choose the category themselves, and DOT has told airlines that some passengers pick categories their written complaint does not support, one reason it redesigned the complaint form on 10 February 2026.

## Which US Airlines Get the Most Complaints?
DOT lists every US airline that drew at least five complaint cases. From January to June 2026, **American Airlines had 9,046**, followed by Delta Air Lines with 4,534 and United Airlines with 4,524.
</> Embed
_**Source:** DOT, Air Travel Consumer Report, August 2026 (Table 3, January to June 2026). Passengers usually file against the airline brand on their ticket, so counts can include flights run by regional partners; Hawaiian Airlines is included in Alaska Airlines._
Raw counts largely follow size. American was also the biggest of DOT's reporting carriers by passengers, with 101.3 million enplaned in the same period, and our largest North American airlines ranking shows how the carriers compare in size. Frontier Airlines (3,673) and Spirit Airlines (2,053) drew more complaint cases relative to their passenger numbers than the larger carriers, which AirAdvisor's per-passenger calculation in the next chart shows. Each figure is a count of complaints filed with DOT, which describes its complaint data as based on consumer perception.

## Complaints per 100,000 Passengers by US Airline
DOT's current tables give counts only, so AirAdvisor divided each reporting carrier's complaint cases by the passengers DOT reports it enplaned from January to June 2026. **Spirit Airlines (27.8)** and **Frontier Airlines (21.1)** had the highest rates; **Southwest Airlines (1.5)** had the lowest.
</> Embed
_**Source:** AirAdvisor calculation from DOT ATCR, August 2026: complaint cases (Table 3, January to June 2026) divided by enplaned passengers in the denied boarding table for reporting marketing carriers (January to June 2026), times 100,000. Covers all 9 carriers DOT reports as marketing carriers, including branded regional partners._
Across the 9 carriers combined, AirAdvisor's calculation gives **6.5** complaint cases per 100,000 passengers, so Southwest's rate was less than a quarter of it and Spirit's more than four times it. Spirit stopped flying on 2 May 2026, so its passenger count covers about four months while complaints kept arriving; 680 of its 2,053 cases were about refunds. JetBlue (9.9) and American (8.9) were the only other carriers above that combined rate. The passenger base excludes inbound international passengers, which raises the rate for airlines with large international networks.

## Outlook
Complaint cases are running at about **7,390 a month** in 2026, against 5,816 a month in late 2025, and DOT now publishes 2026 complaint cases in 12 categories for every listed airline, the more detailed data it promised when ACERS launched. On 24 April 2026, DOT issued a final rule requiring covered airlines to file a one-page summary of passenger rights on delays, cancellations, baggage and boarding and to post it on their websites. Its Aviation Consumer Protection Advisory Committee was scheduled to meet on 22 and 23 September 2026 to discuss that summary and the airline customer service dashboards required by the 2024 FAA Reauthorization Act. For the scale of the delays behind many of these complaints, see our flight delay passenger impact statistics.

## Methodology Note
All complaint figures come from DOT, which counts written complaints to its Office of Aviation Consumer Protection, not complaints made to airlines. Yearly totals use the newest DOT figure for each year: 15,342 for 2019 (ATCR, February 2021), 102,560, 49,991 and 77,656 for 2020 to 2022 (DOT, April 2023), 96,853 submissions for 2023 and 97,906 for 2024. Earlier editions show slightly different values (102,550 for 2020 and 49,958 for 2021), and the OIG cites 15,332 for 2019; category shares for 2021 use the 49,958 base published with that year's categories. DOT also reports 86,240 submissions for 2022, a wider measure than the 77,656 complaints. The 2025 figure combines 49,502 legacy submissions (January to July, summed from seven monthly files) with 29,080 ACERS complaint cases (August to December), and the January to July 2026 total adds the published January to June figure (43,184) to July (8,544). April 2026 (7,278) comes from the June 2026 ATCR. Because DOT revises some monthly counts, the seven monthly figures sum to 51,739, slightly above the 51,728 year-to-date total used in the text. Complaints per 100,000 passengers are AirAdvisor calculations: January to June 2026 complaint cases for each of the 9 reporting marketing carriers divided by the enplaned passengers DOT reports for them in the same edition's denied boarding table, which counts domestic and outbound international passengers but not inbound international ones; DOT's own pre-2023 rankings used a different base, so the rates are not comparable with them. Rankings refer only to the dataset, period and metric named.

## Methodology Note
Complaints reflect passengers' perceptions, are attributed to the airline brand on the ticket, and in ACERS are categorised by the passengers themselves.

Background
DOT’s Office of Aviation Consumer Protection’s (OACP)  role includes assisting,  
educating, and protecting aviation consumersby reviewing and responding to air  
travel-related consumer complaints, conducting investigations, and enforcing  
aviation consumer protection laws.  As part of OACP’s responsibilities, it has a  
process to address air travel-related consumer complaints(see figure 1).
Figure 1. OACP’s Consumer  Refund Complaint Process Prior to the COVID-19  
Pandemic
a For complaint subject matter covered by a statute or DOT regulation, the airline is instructed to respond to the  
consumer and provide OACP with a copy of the response. Copies of airlines response is  not required by OACP if  
subject matter not covered by statute or DOT regulation.
b A substantive response addresses the specific problem about which the consumer has complained.
c Consent orders direct the violator to cease and desist from the problematic practice, and in many cases assess a  
remedial civil penalty.  
Source: OIG analysis of OACP’s consumer complaint process prior to the COVID-19 pandemic  .

## [PDF page 7]
OACP also operates an online consumer complaint portal. This portal  allows  
consumers to submit complaints, inquiries, and opinions—referred to broadly as  
“consumer submissions”—for service they received or requested from airlines or  
ticket agents, not related to safety or security.  4
When OACP  processes  a consumer complaint, an analyst assigns a code  
specifying the category  of consumer complaint  in the Consumer Complaint  
Application (CCA).  5 An OACP analyst then acknowledges  the complainant and  
forwards it to the airline for response.  Federal regulations  require airlines to  
acknowledge receipt of each complaint within 30 days of receiving it and to send  
a substantive written response to each complainant within 60 days of receiving  
the complaint.  6
An OACP analyst will then analyze the airline’s response to the complaint,  
assigning an enforcement code if the airline has violated consumer protection  
requirements.  If an analyst notices an airline has multiple cases with the same  
issue, a complaint that appears egregious, or a response with misinformation or  
problematic verbiage, OACP’s Transportation Industry Analyst Training and  
Reference Manual  7 directs the analyst to run a report in CCA to determine if there  
are similar complaints.  If analysts find a pattern in the case report, they are  
instructed to discuss the trend with a director, who then consults with a  deputy to  
determine if the matter should be referred to an OACP attorney.
Common refund-related consumer violations  include:
•  When a carrier refuses to refund a fully refundable ticket or does not  
refund in the required timeframe.
•  When a carrier refuses to refund a ticket or the refund is not processed in  
the required timeframe as well as in the event a flight is canceled or  
significantly changed/delayed and the consumer opts not to travel.
•  If the carrier assesses a change fee to a fully refundable ticket or a ticket  
that was required to be refunded because the carrier canceled, changed,  
or significantly delayed a flight.
•  If a consumer is entitled to a refund of a ticket purchased and canceled  
within 24 hours and the carrier denies, delays, or assesses  a change fee to  
refund.

If assigned,  the OACP attorneycontinues to collect information about an airline’s  
alleged unfair and deceptive practices  to determine whether to open an  
investigation. This information may come from OACP analyzing related consumer  
complaints,monitoring websites and advertisements, and reviewing materials  
from airline ticket agents. Consistent with due process, once OACP establishes  
sufficient facts to open an investigation, it  generally sends an investigation letter  
to the airline  .  8  Once OACP has received enough information to determine

If the OACP attorney collects sufficient facts to establish that an airline has

matter fails, OACP may take formal enforcement action  against the airline. The  
office may then either initiate enforcement action for resolution before  an

## What this means for you
Before you book, pull up the latest DOT Air Travel Consumer Report and check one thing first: whether its table is labeled complaints or the wider consumer submissions. A fair comparison stays inside one reporting definition and one period — pairing the 2022 complaint ranking with post-June 2023 submission totals will not work.
Keep your booking confirmation and receipts on file. If a cancellation or significant schedule change leaves you wanting a refund, ask for an automatic refund back to the original payment method. The 2024 refund rule requires it to be prompt and for the full amount owed, and it covers significantly delayed checked bags and paid ancillary services you never received.
One limit worth naming: this is a domestic complaint ranking. It says nothing about how any of these carriers performs on an Asia-Pacific itinerary, and the reviewed material adds no route-specific data.
If the airline won’t resolve a refund, submit the DOT complaint form. The data that ranks carriers is the same data you can add to.
Reporting by
ATC Intelligence
ATC Intelligence is the research division of Air Traveler Club. Backed by 15 years in Asia-Pacific aviation, we don't just report on the regional market; we live and work in it. By pairing AI-driven data with strict human fact-checking, we provide actionable, trustworthy journalism designed to make your trips to Asia smarter and more affordable.
Follow our daily coverage on Google News, Google Discover, and social media.

## Key terms
Complaint rate The complaint rate is the number of consumer complaints the DOT records for an airline per 100,000 passengers that carrier boards. The agency normalizes by boarded passengers so carriers of very different sizes can be compared on one scale instead of by raw complaint totals. Because inquiries and opinions sit outside a complaint count but inside the newer submission measure, the same carrier can look different depending on which figure a report displays.Consumer submissions Consumer submissions are the broader category the DOT began displaying in its airline reports, made up of complaints, inquiries, and opinions. The agency used this measure from the June 2023 reporting period onward, and said complaints had averaged 91% of submissions over the prior three years. In practice that means a submission total covers more ground than a complaint count, so lining the two up across periods distorts any comparison.Air Travel Consumer Report The Air Travel Consumer Report is the DOT’s recurring publication of airline performance data, carrying complaint and consumer-submission figures among other measures. It is the document to check for current numbers, since the 2022 complaint ranking is a fixed historical table rather than a live one. Whichever edition a traveler opens, the label on its table is the deciding detail — a complaint count and a submission total are not interchangeable, and comparing across the two without adjustment misleads.2024 refund rule The DOT’s 2024 refund rule sets out what airlines owe when a trip does not go as planned. It requires a refund to be automatic, prompt, in the original form of payment, and for the full amount owed when a qualifying refund is due. Congress later reinforced the protections through the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024, signed into law on May 16, 2024, giving them a statutory basis beyond the original rule.

## Questions? Answers.
What is the difference between complaints and consumer submissions in DOT reports?  
Consumer submissions include complaints, inquiries, and opinions. Per DOT, complaints averaged 91% of consumer submissions over the preceding three years, so a submission total is broader than a complaint count and the two are not interchangeable.
What does DOT’s 2024 refund rule require airlines to do?  
When a qualifying refund is due, the rule requires it to be automatic, prompt, in the original form of payment, and for the full amount owed. It covers cancellations or significant changes when the passenger declines rebooking, plus significantly delayed checked bags and paid ancillary services that were not provided.
Was any airline fined because of its complaint-rate ranking?  
No qualifying US DOT enforcement action was verified as being driven by a carrier’s 2022 complaint-rate ranking. The agency’s complaint system serves consumer submissions and refund oversight, but the reviewed sources do not tie a fine to a ranking position.
How often does the DOT publish airline complaint data?  
The DOT issues its Air Travel Consumer Report on a recurring basis. The reports retrieved for this piece covered January through May 2024, December 2024, and a February 2025 edition.
